newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazilian Indians put on warpaint to press demands.
newsitem.headline: Brazilian Indians put on warpaint to press demands.

text.p: Indians across Brazil are putting on warpaint and grabbing their bows and arrows to press their demands, but that does not mean they are on the warpath, experts said on Wednesday.

In the northeastern state of Maranhao, Indians from the Guajajara tribe were holding at least 40 people captive to demand road works and improved health and education services. The hostages were passengers on a bus seized six days ago.

Spear-bearing Indians of the Waimiri-Atroari tribe have been blockading Brazil's largest tin mine in Amazonas state for 10 days to demand extra compensation for the use of a road passing through their territory.
Xavante warriors in Brasilia stormed National Indian Foundation (Funai) headquarters on Tuesday and tried to kidnap its leader Julio Gaiger before an army of television cameras.
"The Indian population has a lot of piled-up demands. It's only natural that occasionally the pot will boil over," Gaiger told reporters after his ordeal with the fierce Xavante.
Pressure groups said the conflicts in Maranhao, Amazonas and Brasilia were unrelated incidents with no common cause.

The Xavante, a traditionally warlike tribe that has often managed to squeeze favours from the "white man" in return for peace, were upset about erroneous reports that Funai could be closed down, Gaiger said.

Carlos Alberto Ricardo, head of the independent pressure group Instituto Socioambiental, said the Waimiri-Atroari had a similar "ethic of conflict" and their dispute with the Pitinga mine owners was an old one. He said the Guajajara Indians in Maranhao appeared to some extent to be manipulated by local politicians who, like the Indians, wanted a road asphalted.
"I don't think you can think in terms of headlines reading: 'Indian nations rebel against the government,'" Ricardo told Reuters. "These cases are all very different."
Officials said increased media exposure of Indian issues might have a lot to do with the recent spurt in aggression.

Helio Blak, finance director of mining concern Grupo Paranapanema, which owns the Pitinga tin mine, said negotiations with the 700-strong Waimiri-Atroari community were continuing -- dollar by dollar.
"I think we will have a solution soon, mainly because the media attention has moved elsewhere," he said.
The attempted kidnap of Gaiger by the Xavante took place before hordes of journalists, who had been tipped off.

Ricardo said the spotlight on the Xavante, Waimiri-Atroari and Guajajara was distracting attention from more pressing concerns, like the slow progress of demarcating the lands of Brazil's more than 300,000 Indians.

He said that in Rondonia state there were signs landowners were trying to wipe out isolated tribes and in the Javari Valley on the border with Peru Indians were under attack from "predatory" logging firms.
